derivations.claim: By trichotomy, either $y=0$, $y>0$, or $-y>0$. In the first case $y^2=0$. In either positive case, multiplying the positive element by itself gives a positive square; since $(-y)(-y)=y^2$, this proves $y^2\ge0$, with strict inequality when $y\ne0$.
The hypothesis $r^2=x^2+y^2$ and step 1.1 imply $r^2\ge x^2$.
If $x=r$, then $y^2=r^2-x^2=0$. Step 1.1 shows a nonzero $y$ would have $y^2>0$, so $y=0$; and $x=r\ge0$.
If $x\le0$, then $x\le r$ because $r\ge0$. Otherwise $x>0$. If $r<x$, then $x-r>0$ and $x+r>0$, so $x^2-r^2=(x-r)(x+r)>0$, contradicting step 2.1. Hence $x\le r$ in all cases.

Conversely, if $y=0$ and $x\ge0$, the hypotheses give $r^2=x^2$ with $r,x\ge0$. If $r<x$, then $(x-r)(x+r)>0$, contradicting equality of squares; if $x<r$, then $(r-x)(r+x)>0$, the same contradiction. By trichotomy, $r=x$. Equality holds exactly in the stated case.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.
This fixes the mixed relation as $\{Q^I_\alpha,\bar Q_{\dot\beta J}\}=-2\sigma^\mu_{\alpha\dot\beta}P_\mu\delta^I{}_J$.
On a common dense graded linear domain $\mathcal D$, contained in the domains of every generator product in the bracket table, the operator supercommutator is the displayed algebra bracket.

derivations.claim: In the Countable-Choice representation setup [A1, F2], sum the mixed anticommutator in [F1] over the equal spinor labels $\alpha=\dot\beta$ and over $I=1,\ldots,N$. The Kronecker delta leaves one copy for each flavor, and the Pauli-matrix traces give $\sum_{I=1}^{N}\sum_{\alpha=1}^{2}\{Q^I_\alpha,(Q^I_\alpha)^*\}=-2N\sum_{\mu=0}^{3}\operatorname{tr}(\sigma^\mu)P_\mu=-4N P_0=4N P^0$. The last equality uses $P_0=-P^0$ for the stated metric.

Apply the operator identity from step 1.1 to $\Omega$ and take its inner product with $\Omega$. The common product domain in [F2] makes both products defined. Since the inner product is linear in its first variable and $(Q^I_\alpha)^*$ is the actual adjoint, $\langle Q^I_\alpha(Q^I_\alpha)^*\Omega,\Omega\rangle=\|(Q^I_\alpha)^*\Omega\|^2$ and $\langle (Q^I_\alpha)^*Q^I_\alpha\Omega,\Omega\rangle=\|Q^I_\alpha\Omega\|^2$. The right side is $4N\langle P^0\Omega,\Omega\rangle=4NE_\Omega$ by [F3] and normalization. This proves the asserted sum-of-norms identity.

Every summand in step 2.1 is nonnegative, so $E_\Omega\ge0$. A finite sum of nonnegative real numbers is zero exactly when every summand is zero; hence $E_\Omega=0$ exactly when all $Q^I_\alpha\Omega$ and $(Q^I_\alpha)^*\Omega$ vanish, which is precisely supersymmetry invariance by [F3]. If the state is noninvariant, at least one squared norm is strictly positive, so the identity and $4N>0$ imply $E_\Omega>0$. The argument contains no boundary-neutrality assumption.

derivations.claim: Differentiate the stated polynomial with respect to its three chiral coordinates: $W_1=-k+(y/2)\phi_3^2$, $W_2=m\phi_3$, and $W_3=m\phi_2+y\phi_1\phi_3$. Substituting these derivatives into [F1] gives exactly the displayed potential.

Set $a=|k|$, $b=|m|^2$, $c=|y|$, and $t=|\phi_3|^2\ge0$. Write $\bar k y\phi_3^2=x+iu$, where $x,u\in\mathbb R$, and put $r=|\bar k y\phi_3^2|$. By [F2] and [F3], $r\ge0$, $r^2=x^2+u^2$, and modulus multiplicativity gives $r=act$. Applying [F5] gives $x\le act$, with equality exactly when $u=0$ and $x\ge0$. Expanding the first square gives $\left|k-\frac y2\phi_3^2\right|^2=a^2+\frac{c^2t^2}{4}-x\ge a^2+\frac{c^2t^2}{4}-act$. Adding the second term $bt$ and the nonnegative third square yields $V\ge q(t):=a^2+(b-ac)t+\frac{c^2t^2}{4}$. Equality in this lower bound requires the third square to vanish and, when $ct>0$, requires $\operatorname{Im}(\bar k y\phi_3^2)=0$ and $\operatorname{Re}(\bar k y\phi_3^2)\ge0$, equivalently that $\bar k y\phi_3^2$ is nonnegative real.

Suppose $b\ge ac$. If $c>0$, then $(b-ac)t\ge0$ and $c^2t^2/4\ge0$, with their sum zero only at $t=0$. If $c=0$, then $q(t)=a^2+bt$ and $b>0$, so again its unique minimum occurs at $t=0$. Thus $V\ge a^2$. At $\phi_3=\phi_2=0$, every term except $|k|^2$ vanishes, so the lower bound is attained for every $\phi_1$. Conversely, any minimizing value must have $t=0$; then the third square is $|m\phi_2|^2$, which vanishes only for $\phi_2=0$ since $m\ne0$. These are exactly all the minimizers in this regime.

Suppose $0<b<ac$, so $a,c>0$. Completing the square gives $q(t)=a^2-\frac{(ac-b)^2}{c^2}+\frac{c^2}{4}\left(t-\frac{2(ac-b)}{c^2}\right)^2$. The unique minimizing value of $t\ge0$ is therefore $t_*=2(ac-b)/c^2>0$, and the lower bound is $q(t_*)=a^2-(ac-b)^2/c^2=(b/c)(2a-b/c)$. Since $0<b/c<a$, we have $(b/c)(2a-b/c)>0$, while $a^2-q(t_*)=(a-b/c)^2>0$. Thus this lower bound is positive and strictly below $a^2$.
At each minimizer in step 3.1, $W_1=-k\ne0$. The auxiliary equation in [F1] gives $F^1=-\bar W_1\ne0$; hence the classical F-term order parameter is nonzero at every such pointwise minimum.

Put $\rho=(2k/y)(1-b/(ac))$. It is nonzero because $k,y\ne0$ and $0<b<ac$. By [F4] at least one square root exists; let $\phi_3$ be any root, so $\phi_3^2=\rho$. Since $c=|y|>0$, [F3] and $|yy^{-1}|=|1|=1$ give $|1/y|=1/c$. The real factor $1-b/(ac)=(ac-b)/(ac)>0$ has modulus equal to itself, and $|2|=2$, so $|\rho|=\frac{2a}{c}\frac{ac-b}{ac}=\frac{2(ac-b)}{c^2}=t_*$. Multiplicativity in [F3] now gives $|\phi_3|^2=|\phi_3^2|=|\rho|=t_*$. Also $\bar k y\phi_3^2=\bar k y\rho=\frac{2|k|^2(ac-b)}{ac}=\frac{2a(ac-b)}c=ac t_*>0$. For arbitrary $\phi_1$, set $\phi_2=-y\phi_1\phi_3/m$, which is defined because $m\ne0$. The third square vanishes, and the first-square bound is an equality by [F5], so every such field value attains $q(t_*)$.

Conversely, a global minimizer must have $t=t_*$, since $V\ge q(t)\ge q(t_*)$ and the value $q(t_*)$ is attained in step 4.2. Equality in step 2.1 then forces $m\phi_2+y\phi_1\phi_3=0$ and $ ar k y\phi_3^2=ac t_*=2a(ac-b)/c$ by [F5].
